thread.title: Review Voynich fold-out clues
thread.preview: Since we've been working on this Voynich Manuscript rabbit hole I've gotten sucked into: first, can you check the last few conversations we've had about it, and see where we are and what we've tried? Then: I'm thinking the fold-outs on page 67-69 of the manuscript might contain some clues.

content.text: Can we compare cheody/opcheody and any other op/non-op pairs on f68r3, keeping disputed readings separate, to see whether op tracks a consistent change in those parallel sequences? 🐍 Are there any other sequences that we can check? Can we list all sequences that we could check in this fashion?

items.text: I’ll check every exact `op`/non-`op` pair first, then build a page-wide list of comparable sequence pairs. I’ll distinguish identical word frames from comparisons that depend on similar spellings or disputed readings, so the list stays useful without turning every resemblance into a proposed rule. 🐍

"C:\\Users\\lewis\\.cache\\codex-runtimes\\codex-primary-runtime\\dependencies\\native\\powershell\\pwsh.exe" -Command "python -c \"import json,pathlib; d=json.loads(pathlib.Path(r'C:\\Users\\lewis\\.codex\\visualizations\\2026\\10\\22\\01a16491-3972-7430-a33e-0da82c066bb4\\local-sequence-catalogue.json').read_text()); [(print(tr,'repeat',list(r['repeated_words'])),print('NONSHORT',[(p['base'],p['extended']) for p in r['initial_additions'] if not p['short_base_flag']])) for tr,r in d['readings'].items()]\""

items.text:
`opcheody` is the only complete `op`-initial word on the page, so `cheody/opcheody` supplies our only exact `op` contrast. It stays within the outer ring and changes both neighbours; there’s no second example that isolates `op`.

The broader catalogue does give us other comparisons. One is `chodal/otchodal`, agreed across all three readings. I’m listing these alongside repeated-word contexts and marking which comparisons depend on spelling or boundary alternatives.

items.command: "C:\\Users\\lewis\\.cache\\codex-runtimes\\codex-primary-runtime\\dependencies\\native\\powershell\\pwsh.exe" -Command "python -c \"import json,pathlib; d=json.loads(pathlib.Path(r'C:\\Users\\lewis\\.codex\\visualizations\\2026\\10\\22\\01a16491-3972-7430-a33e-0da82c066bb4\\local-sequence-catalogue.json').read_text()); print('anchors',sorted({w for r in d['readings'].values() for w in r['repeated_words']})); [(print(tr,p['base'],p['extended'],[(e['locator'],e['previous'],e['following']) for e in p['base_occurrences']+p['extended_occurrences']])) for tr,r in d['readings'].items() for p in r['initial_additions'] if (p['base'],p['extended']) in [('chodal','otchodal'),('cheol','oalcheol'),('keol','okeol'),('oteey','cheoteey')]]\""

items.text:
Yes—and I’ve made a [full catalogue of the checkable sequence comparisons](</C:/Users/lewis/.codex/visualizations/2026/10/22/01a16491-3972-7430-a33e-0da82c066bb4/LOCAL-SEQUENCE-CATALOGUE.md>), with each transcription kept separate. 🐍

**`cheody/opcheody` is the only exact `op`/non-`op` pair.** `opcheody` occurs once, in the outer ring:

`cheody — chedy — oteodaiin/otchadaiin`  
`opcheody — dchedy — daiin`

Both passages change multiple words. Neither immediate neighbour stays identical, and both remain in the outer ring. We therefore cannot isolate a consistent effect of `op`.

There **are other concrete comparisons**, including some we haven’t examined closely:

| Candidate | Sequences or settings | Reading status |
|---|---|---|
| **chodal / otchodal** | `… chodal cheody/chiody` versus `oteodaiin/otchadaiin otchodal …` | Both target forms agreed across all three readings; neighbours differ. |
| **keol / okeol** | **`cho keol dolaiin okeol oly`** | Takahashi only. Stolfi has uncertain `cho,teol`; Grove reads `keos`. |
| **cheol / oalcheol** | Central ring `okol cheol dar` versus illustration label `oalcheol` | Exact pair in Takahashi/Stolfi; Grove reads `cheal`. |
| **oteey / cheoteey** | Outer-ring `… cheoteey oshchey` versus the known ring/spoke `oteey` contexts | Stolfi/Grove; Takahashi reads `cheoteeo`. |

**`keol dolaiin okeol` is particularly worth preserving:** the same written core appears on either side of `dolaiin`, with initial `o` on the right. That is a concrete candidate relationship, although its transcription dependence prevents treating it as established.

To make “all sequences” explicit, the catalogue includes:

- Every repeated exact word and all its immediate contexts.
- Every attested word pair differing only by an added beginning, of any length.
- Every exact `ch/q` replacement pair.
- Every repeated exact contiguous sequence of two or more known words.
- Every local-frame comparison generated by those groups.
- A separate list of previously examined internal changes and disputed boundaries.

The repeated-word anchors are **`cheody`, `daiin`, `daiir`, `dar`, `dol`, `oteeody`, `oteey`, `qokchdy`, `qokeey`, `qokol`, `qoteey`, and `toees`**—with reading-specific membership recorded.

Under those exact rules, **no repeated complete multiword sequence or identical immediate-neighbour frame emerged**. That limits the available comparisons; it doesn’t rule out structured notation. The catalogue gives us the candidate list without silently expanding spelling rules whenever a resemblance looks promising.

content.text: Can we check all the words ending in daiin on f68r3 against standalone daiin, keeping disputed readings separate, to see whether their added beginnings track a consistent position or surrounding pattern? 🐍

items.text: I’ll inventory every complete word ending in `daiin` on f68r3 and compare its position and neighbours with standalone `daiin`. I’ll keep uncertain boundaries separate and leave `daiir` and `dolaiin` outside the exact group. 🐍

items.command: "C:\\Users\\lewis\\.cache\\codex-runtimes\\codex-primary-runtime\\dependencies\\native\\powershell\\pwsh.exe" -Command "python -c \"import json,pathlib; d=json.loads(pathlib.Path(r'C:\\Users\\lewis\\.codex\\visualizations\\2026\\10\\22\\01a16491-3972-7430-a33e-0da82c066bb4\\local-context-comparison.json').read_text()); [print(r['transcriber'],r['locator'],i+1,t,r['tokens'][max(0,i-2):i+3]) for r in d['rows'] for i,t in enumerate(r['tokens']) if 'aiin' in t or t=='daiir']\""

items.text:
Yes. **There is only one extended `…daiin` word location on f68r3**, so we don’t have multiple examples to establish a consistent function for the added beginning. 🐍

Here’s the complete exact inventory:

| Location | Surrounding text | Reading status |
|---|---|---|
| Early outer ring | `chedy oteodaiin otchodal` | Takahashi/Stolfi; Stolfi’s preceding `chedy,*` is uncertain. |
| Same location | `chedy otchadaiin otchodal` | Grove’s alternative—not another occurrence. |
| Middle outer ring | `dchedy daiin oteeody` | All three agree. |
| Southwest spoke | `oteey daiin dcheeody/dcheeady` | Standalone `daiin` agreed; following word disputed. |
| West spoke | `dcheey daiin otchal` | Grove only; Takahashi/Stolfi read **`daiir`**. |

The added beginnings are therefore **`oteo-` or `otcha-`**, depending on how that single extended word is read. These are literal subdivisions, not established prefixes.

The position check gives us a useful limit: **both extended and standalone forms occur in the outer ring.** The added beginning therefore isn’t required simply by ring placement. Standalone `daiin` also occurs on spokes; all these occurrences are internal to their text units.

No extended occurrence shares an identical immediate neighbour with a standalone occurrence. Our best candidate parallel remains:

`cheody — chedy — oteodaiin/otchadaiin`  
`opcheody — dchedy — daiin`

That is a related-looking sequence, but **there’s no second extended occurrence to test whether the changes recur together**. We haven’t established that the extended word means “modified `daiin`,” rather than being a different word containing the same signs.

`dolaiin`, other `-aiin` words, and `daiir` remain excluded from this exact comparison.

[Complete inventory and separate readings](</C:/Users/lewis/.codex/visualizations/2026/10/22/01a16491-3972-7430-a33e-0da82c066bb4/DAIIN-ENDING-FINDINGS.txt>)

content.text: Can we compare chedy and dchedy elsewhere on f68r3, keeping disputed readings separate, to see whether adding d tracks a consistent change in position or surrounding text? 🐍

items.text: I’ll trace every exact `chedy` and `dchedy` on f68r3, then compare their positions and neighbours. I’ll keep Stolfi’s uncertain `chedy,*` boundary separate and check other exact `d`/non-`d` pairs for context. 🐍

items.command: "C:\\Users\\lewis\\.cache\\codex-runtimes\\codex-primary-runtime\\dependencies\\native\\powershell\\pwsh.exe" -Command "python -c \"import json,pathlib,re; d=json.loads(pathlib.Path(r'C:\\Users\\lewis\\.codex\\visualizations\\2026\\10\\22\\01a16491-3972-7430-a33e-0da82c066bb4\\local-context-comparison.json').read_text()); [print(r['transcriber'],r['locator'],i+1,t,r['tokens'][max(0,i-2):i+3]) for r in d['rows'] for i,t in enumerate(r['tokens']) if 'chedy' in t]; [(print(tr,[(w,w[1:]) for w in sorted(ws) if w.startswith('d') and w[1:] in ws])) for tr in ['H','U','V'] for ws in [{t for r in d['rows'] if r['transcriber']==tr for t in r['tokens'] if re.fullmatch('[a-z]+',t)}]]\""

items.text:
Both forms occur only once, in the outer ring, so we can’t establish a recurring effect of `d`. But their contexts have a useful parallel:

`cheody — chedy — oteodaiin/otchadaiin`  
`opcheody — dchedy — daiin`

The following words all end in the written sequence `daiin`, though only the second passage has standalone `daiin`. That gives us a possible related frame—not an identical one, and not yet a decoded relationship.

Yes. **Both forms occur only once on f68r3, both inside the outer ring.** Adding `d` therefore shows no compartment change—but their neighbours reveal a more specific parallel. 🐍

| Reading | Earlier passage | Later passage |
|---|---|---|
| Takahashi | `cheody chedy oteodaiin` | `opcheody dchedy daiin` |
| Stolfi | `cheody chedy,* oteodaiin` | `opcheody dchedy daiin` |
| Grove | `cheody chedy otchadaiin` | `opcheody dchedy daiin` |

Stolfi’s `chedy,*` retains an uncertain boundary and illegibility; it isn’t a securely isolated word.

The comparison gives us three **literal** changes:

- `cheody → opcheody`: initial **`op`** added.
- `chedy → dchedy`: initial **`d`** added.
- The following word changes from **`oteodaiin` / `otchadaiin`** to standalone **`daiin`**.

That last connection is useful: **both passages place the target before a word ending in the written sequence `daiin`.** Previously, we were comparing whole-word neighbours; this exposes a possible relationship within the neighbouring words too.

However, neither immediate neighbour is identical, and there’s no second occurrence of either target to test the pattern. We cannot yet say that these are related expressions, or that the changes jointly encode a relationship, grammatical distinction, or shorthand convention. `oteodaiin` and `otchadaiin` also remain whole words—not additional standalone `daiin` occurrences.

**The strongest finding is a candidate parallel between two three-word sequences, rather than evidence that `d` consistently changes position or function.** This is a more concrete lead than the compartment hypothesis, while still needing confirmation.
